s: "Congress shall make no law… prohibiting the free exercise" of religion.

Employment Division v. Smith (1990) held that a neutral, generally applicable law burdening religious practice (there, a peyote ban applied to Native American Church members) does not require strict scrutiny.
This replaced the compelling-interest test of Sherbert v. Verner (1963) and Wisconsin v. Yoder (1972) outside the unemployment-compensation context.
The Religious Freedom Restoration Act (1993) restores strict scrutiny against the federal government (Burwell v. Hobby Lobby, 2014; Tanzin v. Tanvir, 2020, damages available).
RLUIPA protects prisoners and land use (Holt v. Hobbs, 2015).
Title VII requires accommodating employees' religion unless doing so imposes "substantial increased costs" (Groff v. DeJoy, 2023).
